Confidentiality
Which control primarily supports confidentiality?
Encrypting a customer database
Keeping a spare power supply
Checksumming a software download
Load balancing two web servers
Encryption keeps data secret from unauthorised readers. Redundancy supports availability and checksums support integrity.
m
Integrity
Which control best detects unauthorised changes to a file?
Comparing its cryptographic hash with a known-good value
Storing it on a server with two network cards
Compressing it before saving it to disk
Giving it a longer, more descriptive file name
A changed hash reveals modification, which is an integrity check.
m
Availability
Which measure most directly improves availability?
Redundant servers with failover
Encrypting traffic with TLS 1.3
Hashing stored passwords
Signing documents digitally
Redundancy and failover keep services running when one component fails.
d
Triad tensions
A bank adds strict account lockout after three failed logins. Which risk does this create?
Attackers can lock legitimate users out deliberately, harming availability
Passwords become readable by anyone on the network
Transactions can be altered without being detected
Logs stop recording failed login attempts
Lockout protects confidentiality but can be abused for denial of service. Designers balance both, for example with progressive delays.
m
AAA
What do the three A's in the AAA framework stand for?
Authentication, authorisation and accounting
Access, audit and availability
Assets, attacks and alerts
Approval, assurance and administration
AAA verifies identity, grants permissions and records actions.
d
AAA order
Why must authentication come before authorisation?
Permissions can only be decided once the system knows who is asking
Authorisation checks are slower, so they are performed last
Authentication is optional when authorisation is strict
Authorisation creates the account that authentication then verifies
Authorisation decisions depend on a verified identity; without it, permissions would be granted to an unknown party.
m
Accounting
What is the purpose of accounting in AAA?
Recording who did what and when
Calculating the cost of security tools
Encrypting data before it is stored
Granting users their access rights
Accounting produces the audit trail used for investigation and accountability.
d
Non-repudiation
Which mechanism provides non-repudiation for an electronic approval?
A digital signature made with the approver's private key
A shared password known to the whole approval team
A symmetric key held by both sender and receiver
An email sent from a shared departmental mailbox
Only the private-key holder can create the signature, so the signer cannot plausibly deny it. Shared secrets cannot prove which person acted.
m
Least privilege
What does the principle of least privilege require?
Giving each user only the access needed for their job
Giving all staff the same access to keep things simple
Giving administrators access to every system by default
Removing access only after a security incident occurs
Minimal access limits the damage a compromised or careless account can do.
d
Just-in-time access
How does just-in-time (JIT) privilege support least privilege?
Elevated rights are granted only for a limited time when needed
Administrators keep permanent rights but must log in more often
Every user receives admin rights at the start of each day
Privileges are granted automatically to anyone who requests them
JIT removes standing privilege, shrinking the window in which stolen admin credentials are useful.
d
Privilege creep
An employee who moved departments three times still has access from every previous role. What is this called?
Privilege creep
Defence in depth
Separation of duties
Fail-safe default
Access accumulates without removal. Regular access reviews counter privilege creep.
m
Defence in depth
What is the core idea of defence in depth?
Multiple independent layers so one failure does not cause compromise
One very strong perimeter firewall that blocks all attacks
Placing all security tools on a single central server
Hiding systems so attackers cannot find them
Layers such as perimeter, endpoint, detection and data controls back each other up.
d
Layer independence
Why should security layers be diverse and independent?
A single flaw or bypass should not defeat several layers at once
Diverse products are always cheaper than one platform
Independent layers need no monitoring or maintenance
Regulators forbid using two products from the same vendor
If every layer shares a weakness, one bypass defeats them all. Diversity improves resilience.
m
Zero Trust
What is the core principle of Zero Trust?
Never trust, always verify, regardless of network location
Trust every device inside the corporate network
Verify users once a year during access reviews
Block all remote access to company systems
Zero Trust evaluates every request using identity, device and context, assuming breach.
d
Zero Trust
Why does Zero Trust reject the idea of a trusted internal network?
Attackers who get inside, or insiders, would otherwise move freely
Internal networks are always slower than the internet
Firewalls cannot be placed inside a corporate network
Internal users never need to access sensitive data
Implicit trust inside the perimeter enables lateral movement after one compromise.
m
Zero Trust pillars
Which is one of the commonly cited Zero Trust pillars?
Device health
Office floor plan
Printer colour
Payroll date
Common pillars include identity, devices, network, applications and data.
m
Fail-safe defaults
What does a fail-safe default mean for access control?
Access is denied unless it has been explicitly allowed
Access is allowed unless it has been explicitly denied
Access is granted to anyone during a system failure
Access rules are reset to factory settings each night
Default deny means mistakes or omissions block access rather than expose data.
d
Fail-safe defaults
A firewall's rule engine crashes. Which behaviour follows the fail-safe principle?
It blocks traffic until it recovers
It allows all traffic to avoid an outage
It forwards traffic to a random server
It deletes its configuration file
Failing closed protects assets, although availability needs must be weighed for safety-critical systems.
m
Complete mediation
What does complete mediation require?
Every access is checked, not only the first one
Access is checked once per user per year
Only administrators' access is checked
Access checks are made by the user's manager
Caching an early decision can let revoked access continue; complete mediation checks each request.
d
Secure by default
Why are shipping products with default passwords a design failure?
Attackers can look up the defaults and log in
Default passwords are always too long to remember
Default passwords slow the device's start-up time
Default passwords stop software updates installing
Secure-by-default products force unique credentials. Botnets such as Mirai abused factory default passwords.
m
Separation of duties
What does separation of duties prevent?
One person completing a sensitive task alone without a check
Two people sharing the same desk or office
Employees taking holidays at the same time
Managers reading staff email without consent
Splitting steps, such as raising and approving a payment, means fraud requires collusion.
d
Dual control
How does dual control differ from separation of duties?
Two people must act together on the same step, such as two keys for a vault
One person performs a task while another watches the CCTV later
Two departments write separate policies for the same process
Each person can complete the whole task alone on alternate days
Separation splits steps across people; dual control needs two people for one critical action.
d
Applied cases
In the 2013 Target breach, attackers first entered through a third-party HVAC vendor's credentials. Which principle failure allowed them to reach payment systems?
Insufficient network segmentation and least privilege for vendor access
Lack of encryption on the store's public website
Weak passwords on customers' online accounts
Missing antivirus on the HVAC units themselves
Vendor access should have been confined. Poor segmentation let attackers move toward point-of-sale systems.
d
Applied cases
What does the 2016 Dyn DDoS attack illustrate?
Compromised IoT devices with default credentials can disrupt major services
Encrypted email cannot be read by government agencies
Ransomware spreads mainly through printed documents
Strong passwords alone prevent all denial-of-service attacks
The Mirai botnet used insecure IoT devices to flood Dyn's DNS service, disrupting many websites.
m
Security through obscurity
Why is security through obscurity not enough on its own?
Secrets about design are eventually discovered
Obscurity always makes systems run slower
Obscurity is illegal in most countries
Obscurity cannot be used with encryption
Hiding details may add friction, but security must hold even when the design is known.
m
Usability
Why can overly complex security controls reduce security?
Users create workarounds, such as writing passwords down
Complex controls cannot be audited by anyone
Complex controls are always cheaper to bypass
Complex controls disable logging by design
Usable security matters; friction drives risky behaviour.
d
Applied cases
In the 2021 Colonial Pipeline incident, attackers reportedly used a legacy VPN account without MFA. Which control would most directly have helped?
Multi-factor authentication and removal of unused accounts
A larger internet connection for the pipeline control room
Physical locks on the operator workstations
Faster backup tape drives for the billing system
A single compromised password reached a remote access account; MFA and account hygiene address that path.
m
Principles in practice
A developer's service account has database admin rights but only needs to read one table. Which principle is violated?
Least privilege
Availability
Non-repudiation
Obscurity
The account should have read access to that table only.
d
Assume breach
What does an assume-breach mindset change in how a team designs defences?
It invests in detection, containment and limiting lateral movement
It stops investing in prevention because breaches are inevitable
It disables logging because attackers will delete logs anyway
It relies entirely on the perimeter firewall to stop attackers
Prevention still matters, but planning for compromise leads to segmentation, monitoring and response readiness.
m
Integrity
Why do software publishers sign their downloads?
So users can verify the file came from them unaltered
So the download completes faster over the internet
So the software can run without any user permissions
So the file cannot be copied to another computer
Code signing supports integrity and authenticity of software.
